Slimming in joules not calories
After January 1st 1978 slimmers will need to watch
the joules rather than the calories! The UK is
considering changing from the calorie to the joule as
the unit of measurement for making energy
declarations on food labels and in advertisements. The change arises from the world-wide adoption of
the International System of Units (SI) and is part of
our obligation under the EEC Units of Measurements
Directives.

brief_context: Mentioned regarding its record for deaths from electrocution.
brief_extract: The Department of Prices and Consumer Protection in publishing the figures for 1975 gives an analysis of the trends together with case histories of all the fatal accidents, so that much may be learned to provide for greater safety in the home. It is encouraging to note that the record in the United Kingdom for deaths from electrocution is one of the best in Europe as far as comparable statistics are available. In 1975 there were 126 deaths from all causes directly or indirectly associated with electricity in the home and this compares with 141 in the previous year.

A parallel may be drawn with the increased safety when electric lighting took over from candles and oil lamps in bedrooms.

brief_context: Only country with similar accident data available before this survey.
brief_extract: By mid-1977 the Safety Research Section of the DPCP will have built up sufficient data to provide detailed information related to home accidents such as types and place of accident, products involved, and age groups most at risk. It will be the first time that such data have been available in this country, and, with the exception of the United States, the first time that they have been available anywhere in the world. Almost a quarter of a million people have died in home accidents since the last war.

brief_context: Introducing a pilot accident survey scheme based on the UK.
brief_extract: Almost a quarter of a million people have died in home accidents since the last war. Considerable interest has been shown by other countries, and the Scandinavian countries are introducing a pilot scheme based largely on that in the UK. Such information is valuable to BSI technical committees in deciding the provisions for proposed regulations concerning, for instance, perambulators and push chairs.

brief_context: International trade and standardisation context across European regions.
brief_extract: The EAW has always laid great stress on the safe use of electrical equipment and is ever willing to give advice and information through its Headquarters and through its branch network. In view of the development of international trade, particularly in Europe, much work has been done on the harmonisation of standards so that a British housewife and her European counterpart should be able to use equipment from whatever source with the same confidence. In this work, too, the EAW has taken an important part through representation on committees of the British Standards Institution and participation in standards conferences overseas.

CEE System
The CEE system is used in most European countries but it too has many variations. It is found in the former French African territories, Russia, Argentina, Brazil and Chile; the exceptions are the UK, Denmark and Switzerland. One type of socket outlet called Schuko is widely used in Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden and Finland, the other in Belgium, France and Czechoslovakia.

brief_context: Destination for supply flights from Christchurch.
brief_extract:
Today
19 nations share information, equipment,
people and ideas regarding a frozen continent
covering 7 million cubic miles with 51 bases. A year round facility is maintained at
Christchurch where personnel and supplies are
prepared for the 2,300 mile flight south to
Williams Field, 8 miles from McMurdo Sound
by large US C141 Starlifters and NZ C130
Hercules aircraft during the operational season
between September and February. Supplies
include heavy machinery and equipment,
catering, mail and everything to sustain the
bases for the long season.

VISIT TO DIDCOT POWER STATION
by Mrs M. Braithwaite, Magazine Secretary, Reading Branch

On arrival members were taken into the lecture
room for a film showing the building of the power
station, the first unit of which came into operation in
September 1970. The film explained, in simple
terms, the generating of electricity.

brief_context: used as a size comparison for power generation
brief_extract:
As they went along the gallery looking down
on to the turbines and generators, the guides
explained in detail the work of each part and how the
resultant electricity is fed to the National Grid. The
station can produce enough electricity to meet the
needs of ten cities as big as Oxford. After this members visited the Observers' Bay
which overlooks the control room with its panels of
switches, coloured alarm systems and television
monitor screens, all of which prompted many
questions.

brief_context: Mentioned regarding the potential price increase of goods.
brief_extract: A request for cheap appliances which could be thrown out once a fault occurred was viewed with horror by the manufacturers who said that they were prevented from producing "cheap and nasty" products by the safety regulations and that even if they could do so for this country, the safety regulations of the export markets would prohibit them. If they lost their export markets, 35% of the labour force would have to go and the price of UK goods would rocket. One recommendation which received unanimous support was for a checklist of what could be wrong with an appliance.

brief_context: Mentioned regarding energy needs and fuel reserves.
brief_extract: TOMBS, Chairman, Electricity Council, at the EAW Annual General Meeting. “OUR present energy needs in the United Kingdom amount to a total of about 350 million tons of coal equivalent per year and it is generally estimated that this figure will rise to something approaching 500 million tons of coal equivalent by the year 2000 if the economic state of the country is to support the aspirations of its population. We are fortunate in having very large reserves of coal which will last us for some hundreds of years, but the most optimistic estimates of production in the year 2000 are around 130m tons per year and even to produce this will require an investment of about £4,000m”.

There is widespread confusion between nuclear weapons and nuclear electrical power. Problems of Storage
Regarding the problems of storing the active wastes from irradiated fuel it is noteworthy that the existence of highly active wastes is not a new phenomenon; traces of naturally occurring nuclear reactors some millions of years old have been discovered in Africa. The problem of safe storage is eminently capable of solution.

LIFE IN THE DEEP SOUTH

SUSI LUSS interviews MERIEL LLOYD on her visit to the Southern States of the USA

A Georgia Plantation house

MERIEL LLoyd, the EAW Membership Liaison Officer, spent an exciting month in the Southern States of America in January this year. She went primarily to visit friends, to ski in the Appalachian Mountains, to explore Disneyland in Florida, and to absorb a very different way of life, but she also never forgot her involvement with the EAW and returned full of news which I hope will be of interest to all readers of The Electrical Age.

cope with the intense cold, we were scraping the
ice off the inside of the car windscreen. Americans started appreciating the gravity of

one to two week's heating oil in advance.

brief_context: Country visited by David Hyde for equipment demonstration trips.
brief_extract:
Then, aged fifteen, he
broke his neck and he has been a tetraplegic
ever since. David has done more than just cope
with his severe physical disability — he is living
proof of how highly sophisticated equipment can
make a severely disabled person independent
and able to earn a living, including travelling on
demonstration trips to countries as distant as
Russia and Australia. POSSUM, formed from the initials POSM
standing for Patient Operated Selection
Mechanism and which in Latin means "I can"
or "I am able", is the first form of equipment
specially designed to enable severely disabled
people to exercise efficient and effortless control
over electrical and electro-mechanical
equipment thus giving them the possibility of
employment, education, communication and
recreation.

brief_extract: What should I look for? In Britain the voltage in the domestic household is standardised at 240 volts. However, within the Common Market countries there can be several different voltages in one country.

brief_context: Reference to varying voltages within European Common Market countries.
article_title: I want to give hair care equipment to my niece who is going abroad. What should I look for?
brief_extract: In Britain the voltage in the domestic household is standardised at 240 volts. However, within the Common Market countries there can be several different voltages in one country. Where the voltage is much lower, the appliance will not work properly.

brief_context: Mention of dual voltage appliances usually found in Europe.
article_title: I want to give hair care equipment to my niece who is going abroad. What should I look for?

It would be useful to check on the voltage in the country where your niece is going to work.

brief_context: Mentioned regarding the prevalence of poorly lit homes.
brief_extract:
THE LIGHT OF YOUR LIFE

Rise and fall U122 by Conelight in enamelled white or anodised silver (not shown)

As the days draw in and we can no longer luxuriate in the soft glow of summer evenings we suddenly realise how dependent we are on artificial lighting and notice pools of gloom in a room we once thought bright and cheery. Five out of six homes in Britain are still considered by experts to be poorly lit. Surprising, when good lighting, well placed, can enhance the appearance of a room.

brief_context: Mentioned in the context of Yorkshire Pudding.
brief_extract: With the movement of population most dishes have travelled to nearly every part of the country. Over the years there have been variations on a popular dish, or, as in the case of Yorkshire Pudding, most cooks have used the same recipe but have argued over how it should be cooked and served. The following are just a few of the many recipes which owe their title to a town or county.

SCOTLAND
Scotland is the home of Shortbread but many of us have our own pet variations on the basic recipe of 6 oz flour, 4 oz butter and 2 oz sugar. These often include replacing some of the flour with either rice flour or cornflour.

brief_context: The region whose culinary tradition for lamb is introduced.
brief_extract:
WALES
Renowned for its succulent lamb, of which the choicest cuts are best roasted or grilled and served with simple vegetables, such as potatoes and peas and a touch of mint sauce, rosemary or redcurrant jelly. The cheaper cut, breast of lamb, needs to be carefully selected to ensure that a meaty, rather than an over fatty cut, is bought.

brief_context: Location of the factory where SONA kettles are manufactured.
article_title: Up the Spout: Your Electric Kettle from Start to Finish
brief_extract: Always a curious soul, I was interested to learn how my automatic kettle started out in life and NC Joseph Limited, whose brand name is SONA, invited me to follow the progress of coils of metal transformed stage by stage into the handsome, gleaming finished article which helps provide the nation with its mainstay — the Great British ‘Cuppa’! The plant in Stratford-on-Avon, from which the SONA name is derived (simply the ‘S’ on ‘A’), is not designed like a huge hangar although the overall production area is around 150,000 sq. ft.

brief_context: Location from where electrical cables connect to the island.
article_title: ELECTRICITY ON THE ISLE OF WIGHT
brief_extract: We then went to the main intake site at Wootton which is unmanned although inspections do take place frequently. We were shown the huge transformers and were told that three cables connect the island to Fawley. One cable could handle the current for the island adequately — although two are always in use, with the third in reserve.

brief_context: Emergency contact point for the island's electricity supply.
article_title: ELECTRICITY ON THE ISLE OF WIGHT
brief_extract:
The consumers on the island, however, cover the cost of this with their individual bills. Members then learnt that in an emergency, contact can be made between the island and Portsmouth, so help is always available. This was a most instructive and memorable outing, and we all came away feeling deeply impressed by the sophistication of the equipment and the efficiency of the personnel.”

brief_context: Location of a branch commenting on the value of complaints.

EUROPEAN CHRISTMAS

WHEN researching for recipe pages for this Christmas issue, I rapidly came to the conclusion that to be truly appreciated, the dishes we would present to you would have to be put into their local and national contexts and I hope, in the next few paragraphs, to sketch out how our European cousins celebrate Christmas. Gemütlichkeit —

the German Christmas Spirit

The Christmas season starts early in Germany — invariably with the first Sunday in Advent (four Sundays before Christmas) when most German families start thinking of Christmas and buy a pine wreath decorated with red ribbons and candles for the table. Each Sunday before Advent, one of the candles is lit — all part of the gradual build-up to Christmas.

brief_context: Identified as the place where the Christmas tree originated.
article_title: EUROPEAN CHRISTMAS: Gemütlichkeit — the German Christmas Spirit
brief_extract: On December 5th, the eve of St Nicholas Day, children in Germany hang their stockings on a door handle or leave a pair of boots or shoes near a window, in the hope that St Nicholas will reward them with presents for good behaviour during the past year. The Christmas tree originated in Strasbourg during the 17th Century (when Strasbourg was part of Germany) where small fir trees were decorated with cakes, sweets, fruit and paper. When Prince Albert brought this tradition over to England, Queen Victoria and her people adopted it and made it one of their own.

brief_context: Country whose Christmas food traditions are extensively described.
brief_extract: The Réveillon can be anything from a light supper to a large dinner. More substantial food may be kept for the Christmas Day lunch and the Réveillon often includes shell-fish, especially oysters, which are a great favourite in France. Foie gras — a goose liver pâté — might be served on this occasion too.

brief_context: Region mentioned in relation to fine wine selection.
brief_extract: In France not everyone chooses turkey and many a family delights in some other type of fowl, such as guinea fowl, goose, duck or even game like pheasant or partridge. Traditionally, roast chestnuts will accompany the poultry, with sprouts or cabbage and special care will be taken in choosing the wine — a claret, a château-bottled one perhaps, or a fine Burgundy. Champagne is also part of the celebrations — either served as an apéritif, or drunk throughout the meal but always offered at the end of the meal before coffee.

brief_context: Country where the Advent wreath and other customs are described.
brief_extract: Every day the candle is lit to burn away the portion for the previous day. The Advent wreath is a Northern European tradition — in Denmark the wreath is hung with red ribbons from the ceiling or placed in a special holder so that it can be placed on the table. Often a few small decorations such as silver bells, miniature straw goats, or glass balls are attached to it.

brief_context: Location where ancient straw mobiles can be seen.

brief_context: Country where the Christmas traditions described are practiced.
brief_extract: Every town has its large, illuminated fir tree in the main square, and nearly every house has one too. It is usually more richly decorated in Denmark than here, and many people still prefer the soft light of small, wax candles rather than electric ones. There are many small presents on the tree, and often strings of the red and white Danish flag, the Dannebrog.

brief_context: Region in Denmark where Nisser are particularly prominent.
brief_extract: This is followed by distribution of the presents. The mythical Nisser plays an important part in the Danish Christmas, particularly in Jutland and in the country districts. These are goblin-like characters dressed in red and grey doublets, red hose, and a small red cap with the point hanging down on one side.

VISIT AT FAWLEY POWER STATION
by Mrs R. M.

brief_context: Region whose electricity needs are met by the station.
brief_extract: It first supplied power to the grid in 1969. It has four generating units, each of which produces 500,000 kW - about the total need of Hampshire. When the station is running at full capacity the output is 2,000,000 kW, and at any one time can produce 1/20th of the country's electricity.

brief_context: The power station is one of the largest in Europe.
brief_extract: Before the tour they were given a talk on generating electricity and the function of power stations, in particular, Fawley. Fawley Power Station is the first of its kind under computer control and is also one of the largest stations in Europe. It first supplied power to the grid in 1969.

location_standardised: Test, River, Hampshire, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: River supplying pure water to Fawley Station boilers.
brief_extract: The water is very warm when it is discharged into the sea and as a result a thriving bed of oysters has established itself. The boilers also require 5 million gallons of pure water which is piped from the rivers Test and Avon and demineralised before reaching the boilers. Fawley Station stands in 175 acres of land which has mostly been reclaimed from the sea.

'ELECTRICITY IN THE COMMUNITY' — LEEDS BRANCH EXHIBITION
by Miss Winifred Porter, Magazine Secretary, Leeds Branch
When members of Leeds Branch discussed their programme for the theme 'EAW in the Community', suggestions naturally centred on the local city, Leeds. We knew that at least four sales women from some of the electrical shops in the city had obtained their Home Electricity certificates through a Leeds Branch and when a local exhibition was suggested it was natural that we should bear this in mind when considering where and how it could be held.

brief_context: Region mentioned in relation to Schofields department store.
article_title: 'ELECTRICITY IN THE COMMUNITY' — LEEDS BRANCH EXHIBITION
brief_extract: We knew that at least four sales women from some of the electrical shops in the city had obtained their Home Electricity certificates through a Leeds Branch and when a local exhibition was suggested it was natural that we should bear this in mind when considering where and how it could be held. We deputised a member to try and organise such an event and aiming high she approached the Manager of the electrical department of the leading department store in Leeds, Schofields (Yorkshire) Ltd. He was very interested in the scheme and immediately co-operated.

brief_context: Site of the BEAB appliance testing laboratories.
article_title: 'ELECTRICITY IN THE COMMUNITY' — LEEDS BRANCH EXHIBITION
brief_extract: At the request of the West Yorkshire Police, who provided crime prevention leaflets, Chubb Burglar alarms were demonstrated to show the progress of electronic protection devices. BEAB provided literature on their safety testing which was placed on all the approved appliances in the store and they also sent some colour photographs of their appliance testing laboratories in Leatherhead. We are very grateful to all these firms, boards and organisations for their really wonderful and generous co-operation.
